articles.title: Hopwood Hall College celebrates topping out of new Clegg Building
articles.excerpt: A topping out ceremony at Hopwood Hall College marks a significant step in the construction of the new Clegg Building, set to enhance educational facilities in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A topping out ceremony was held at Hopwood Hall College on October 26, 2026, marking a significant milestone in the construction of the new Clegg Building. This event celebrated the completion of the building's structure, which is being developed by Willmott Dixon and funded by the Department for Education, Rochdale Council, and the college itself.

The ceremony was attended by notable figures including Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE, Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, and the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale, Faisal Rana and Iram Faisal.

Family members of the late Robert Clegg OBE, after whom the building is named, were also present, highlighting the personal connection to the college. Robert Clegg served as Chair of the Corporation from 2007 to 2018 and made significant contributions during his tenure.

During the event, attendees were taken to the roof of the new building, which offers panoramic views of the borough, including landmarks such as Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Parish Church.

Guests were invited to leave messages on the roof parapet, creating a lasting record of the occasion.

The Clegg Building is expected to provide a modern and inspiring learning environment for students at Hopwood Hall College, enhancing educational opportunities in the area.

As construction progresses, the college community looks forward to the completion of this landmark development, which aims to foster a better learning experience for current and future students.

An eight-year-old school pupil has won a competition to name a road for a new £6.4 million First Choice Homes Development in Heywood. Ava McEvoy put forward the name Murphy Close for the housing association’s 27-home Bury Old Road project in honour of a local Catholic priest. A panel of judges decided the year 4 student’s suggestion will now take pride of place at the development's entrance. Father Morris Murphy founded a parish for the Darnhill Estate in the 1960s and was a respected community figure until his death in 2013. Ava, who goes to Our Lady and St Paul's RC Primary School, received a Samsung tablet for her winning name. "I'm really happy that my street name was chosen," she said. FCHO project and partnerships officer Ghazalla Ibqal said: "This competition has given local children the opportunity to leave a lasting mark on the neighbourhood while learning about the people and stories that have helped shape Heywood. “We'd like to thank the school for working with us and congratulate Ava on her fantastic entry." The Bury Old Road project by Built Developments for FCHO comprises 12 two-bedroom and 15 three-bedroom properties. Nineteen are for social rent and eight rent-to-buy. Completion is scheduled for May next year. articles.title: Rochdale awards event recognises achievements of over 200 cared for children
articles.excerpt: More than 200 children in care were celebrated at an awards event hosted by Rochdale Borough Council, recognising their achievements and resilience.
articles.content_html:
More than 200 cared-for children were celebrated at an awards event hosted by Rochdale Borough Council. The ceremony took place recently and aimed to acknowledge the determination and resilience of these young individuals, who were nominated for their outstanding achievements in extracurricular activities.

A total of 273 nominations were received for the awards, highlighting the diverse talents and efforts of the children involved.

Awards were presented to those who exemplified role model behaviour and showed exceptional determination in their pursuits, reinforcing the positive impact these children have within their communities.

The event featured various fun activities designed to entertain the children and their families, creating a joyful atmosphere. Local sponsors supported the council in organising the event, which is part of Rochdale Borough Council's annual activities to celebrate the achievements of children in care.

Families and carers attended the awards event alongside the children, making it a community-focused occasion. The event also included character appearances, adding an element of excitement for the young attendees.

This recognition not only celebrates the children's achievements but also aims to inspire them to continue striving for success in their future endeavours.

articles.title: Planning approved for new £11.4 million special needs school in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has received planning permission to build a new special needs school, set to open in 2028, aimed at supporting children with complex needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has been granted planning permission to construct a new special needs school, designed to accommodate pupils with complex educational needs. The £11.4 million project will be located on a site off Mayfield Street and will serve as a satellite for Redwood School, focusing on children with autism and social-emotional challenges related to autism.

The new school will provide 64 places for students aged 11 to 16 and is expected to open its doors on September 1, 2028. The development will include a part one, two, and three-storey split-level building, complete with parking, play areas, and landscaped grounds.

The aim is to create a secure and therapeutically informed learning environment that supports vulnerable young people.

Seven Architecture, the firm behind the design, stated that the facility will enhance the quality of special educational needs (SEN) provision within the borough.

The school will feature a café and spaces designed to foster personal development and effective behaviour management, ensuring that staff can deliver specialist teaching in a supportive setting.

Construction is set to begin next year, marking a significant step forward in expanding educational resources for children with special needs in Rochdale.

This initiative is crucial for local families seeking tailored educational support for their children, reflecting the council's commitment to improving SEN services in the area.

Planning permission has been granted for Rochdale Council to create a 64-place alternative provision school on lane off Mayfield Street in Rochdale, as a satellite site for Redwood School for children with complex autism and social-emotional needs related to autism. Work is due to start next year and the school — a Raise Rochdale Pupil Referral School — is due to open September 1, 2028. The vacant former farmland will see a part one, two and three-storey split-level school created, including parking, play areas and landscaping. In documents submitted with the planning application, Seven Architecture said: “This development will deliver a specialist educational facility for pupils aged 11-16 with social, emotional and mental health needs — supporting the council’s objective to expand high-quality SEN provision within the borough. “The proposed scheme will provide accommodation for up to 64 pupils, creating a cafe, secure and therapeutically informed learning environment designed to support vulnerable young people. “The development seeks to deliver a high-quality educational setting that enables staff to effectively manage behaviour, support personal development and deliver specialist teaching within a carefully planned and supportive environment. Image: Seven Architecture “The Raise Rochdale Pupil Referral School is managed by Rochdale Council and it is where children are educated if they have been excluded from mainstream schools. “Most children on roll at Raise Rochdale do have special educational needs, but they don’t meet the criteria for special school.” The number of children on roll at Raise Rochdale has risen from 68 in October, 2014, to 199 in May, 2025. After leasing a site and plans for a permanent school falling through, last year the council approved the creation of a new school to accommodate increasing numbers needed by Raise Rochdale Pupil Referral Service. Seven Architecture added: “This scheme will deliver a new school for 64 pupils specifically designed for Raise Rochdale PRS. articles.title: Two drivers have vehicles seized for ignoring Heywood school crossing patrol
articles.excerpt: Two vehicles were seized by police in Heywood after drivers ignored a school crossing patrol, highlighting ongoing concerns about road safety near schools.
articles.content_html:
Police in Heywood have seized two vehicles after drivers failed to stop for a school crossing patrol. The incident occurred when Mr. Jones, the crossing patrol officer, was already standing in the road as the vehicles approached.

No injuries were reported during these incidents.

The vehicles seized included a moped and a silver Skoda. Police collected evidence, including witness statements, before taking action.

This incident is part of a broader concern, as there have been 137 reported cases of vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols in the Rochdale area.

Councillor Williams expressed his dismay at the incidents, stating that such behaviour is unacceptable and poses a significant risk to children. In response to these ongoing safety issues, police have been using body-worn cameras in hotspot areas to deter dangerous driving.

The seizure of these vehicles underscores the need for increased vigilance and compliance with road safety regulations, particularly near schools. Local residents and parents are encouraged to remain alert and report any similar incidents to the authorities.

articles.excerpt: St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was closed after a bomb threat, with all students and staff accounted for and safe. The school plans to reopen on Monday.
articles.content_html:
St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was closed on Friday following a bomb threat that prompted an immediate response from Greater Manchester Police. Emergency services evacuated all school buildings as a precautionary measure, ensuring the safety of students and staff.

During the incident, all students and staff were accounted for, and the school confirmed that there was no actual threat or danger to anyone present. Parents were reassured about the situation, particularly in light of speculation circulating on social media regarding intruders or weapons.

The police responded swiftly to the threat, and after thorough checks, it was determined that there was no risk to the school community.

The school administration has communicated with parents to clarify the situation and dispel any false rumors that may have arisen during the incident.

St Cuthbert’s RC High School is expected to reopen as usual on Monday, allowing students to return to their regular schedule. The incident highlights the importance of safety protocols in schools and the effective response of emergency services in such situations.

Late applications are considered after National Offer Day, 1 March 2027. Schools do not hold places back for late applicants, so a preferred school may already be full.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s evacuated as message reassures parents all children and staff are safe
articles.excerpt: St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust says St Cuthbert’s was evacuated following a possible bomb threat. All children and staff are safe; parents can collect pupils.
articles.content_html:
Latest update — St Teresa of Calcutta trust statement

St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees St Cuthbert’s RC High School, has released a statement saying staff received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat on Friday morning, 16 October.

The trust says emergency services were called, all school buildings were evacuated as a precaution and Greater Manchester Police attended. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, it says.

Parents and carers can now collect their children or give consent for them to travel home, according to the statement. The trust says specialist security operatives will carry out a full sweep of the building this afternoon. It currently expects the school to reopen as normal on Monday 19 October, subject to further updates.

The trust’s account conflicts with some earlier reports circulating about the incident. In particular, it describes rumours of intruders or weapons on school premises as false. Earlier references to a lockdown should be read alongside this latest statement, which describes a precautionary evacuation following a possible bomb threat.

This remains a developing story. Rochdale Daily will continue to update this article with official information as it is released. The earlier updates below are retained for context; the latest trust statement takes precedence where accounts differ.

Trust statement in full:

Earlier this morning (Friday 16 October 2026), staff at St. Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises.

The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure.

All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures.

Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present.

We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority.

Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required.

Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received.

Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home.

We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter.

We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises.

More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with GMP and Rochdale Borough Council.

Source: Statement attributed to St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026.

Earlier updates — before the trust statement

Developing update — councillor requests official briefing

Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short has said he is urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police following reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School. In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, he said he first learned of the reports through the Manchester Evening News and had not received an official briefing.

His statement does not establish what prompted the incident. The earlier message shared with Rochdale Daily described a precautionary evacuation and said all children and staff were safe and accounted for.

Councillor Tarrant-Short’s statement in full:

I want to address the reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School.

First and foremost, my thoughts are with the children, their families and the staff. I understand how frightening this situation will be, particularly for parents waiting for information and reassurance.

I want to be clear: I first became aware of this through the Manchester Evening News. I have not received an official briefing.

I am now urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police so I can understand what has happened and what support is being provided to those affected.

Having been through a similar situation myself when Newhouse Academy went into lockdown, I know how distressing that uncertainty can feel. Behind every update are children who may be frightened and families desperate to know their loved ones are safe.

I am asking that communication with families is timely, clear and compassionate, and that support is available for anyone left distressed.

Until there is verified information, I will not speculate about the circumstances. Please follow official updates from the school and police, and avoid sharing rumours.

The immediate priority must be the safety and wellbeing of every child and member of staff.

Earlier report

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale has been evacuated as a precaution, according to a message to parents and carers shared with Rochdale Daily.

The message states: “All children and staff are safe and accounted for.”

It reassures families that pupils’ safety and wellbeing remain the school’s “absolute priority” and says staff are managing the situation in line with established procedures.

Parents and carers have been told they will receive another communication as soon as further information is available.

The message does not explain what prompted the evacuation or give instructions for collecting children.

St Cuthbert’s is on Shaw Road in Rochdale. The school’s website is https://www.stcuthberts.stoccat.org.uk/.

This is a developing story.

articles.title: Future of College Bank towers uncertain as renovation could take over a decade
articles.excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the College Bank tower blocks would displace residents for more than ten years, with no decision yet made on their future.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed that no decision has been made regarding the future of the College Bank tower blocks, known locally as the Seven Sisters. However, housing officials have warned that any renovation of the iconic structures would require residents to vacate their homes for over a decade.

The Seven Sisters, which have stood for 61 years, are in urgent need of modernisation. Residents have been advocating for refurbishment rather than demolition, and recently appealed to Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig for support in their campaign.

If the renovation proceeds, RBH has indicated that the buildings would not be habitable until the extensive work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in 2017 when RBH expressed concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their lifespan.

In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping that a partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would lead to restoration. However, in September 2024, it was announced that this partnership would not continue, prompting further calls for assistance from local leaders.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Following safety surveys conducted in October 2025, RBH declared that the blocks were unsafe for occupancy, necessitating the relocation of residents.

As the situation develops, the community awaits clarity on the next steps for the future of their homes.

But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes. Campaigners refute the claims and have used Freedom of Information Act requests for Building Safety Regulator documents relating to College Bank and Lower Falinge. The tenants union said: “It is clear from these documents and statements that for the past two years RBH has been unable or unwilling to comply with the Building Safety Regulator’s requirements for an action plan to address issues which need to be resolved in the medium term at College Bank. “This includes straightforward basic repairs, cyclical maintenance and issues that would be addressed in any refurbishment plan.” While RBH says no decision on the future of the College Bank tower blocks has been taken, campaigners want the demolition of Lower Falinge properties to stop. The landmark College Bank tower blocks dominate Rochdale’s skyline The tenants union said: “None of the Lower Falinge residents the campaigners have spoken to want this demolition to go ahead, not least because it will decimate the beautiful urban greenspace and considerable biodiversity in the town centre estate. “RBH refuses to explain why refurbishment is considered too expensive an option. Instead it prefers to continually make unfounded assertions that the homes in Lower Falinge are ‘end-of-life’, that they ‘cannot be occupied’, and that they mysteriously can ‘no longer provide safe, warm homes’ for residents. “Residents on both estates can see that RBH has deliberately created unfit and unsafe homes through managed decline of housing that they were entrusted with when all the council’s housing was transferred to it in early 2012.” College Bank resident Ann Jones said: “At a consultation workshop in 2017, one of RBH’s architects was attempting to steer me towards choosing the option for College Bank which involved demolition. READ MORE: Police officer sentenced for injuring pedestrian in high-speed crash Vacant blocks on the Lower Falinge estate. Image: Google “This was their aim back then. Today, citing the structural surveys whilst withholding their content, to get people out, is the latest device to try and achieve the demolition of over 750 homes on College Bank alone, while they also intend to demolish over 140 homes on Lower Falinge. This is completely unacceptable in a housing crisis.” Lower Falinge tenant Andrew Roche said: “I love living on Falinge, and the prospect of losing my home to RBH’s bulldozers is devastating.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh backed calls for a swift resolution. He said: “Tenants have been left in limbo for far too long and I hope that they can be given the answers they need about the safety and the future of their homes. “I urge RBH to act as swiftly as possible to bring this to a conclusion on behalf of all Rochdale residents during a housing emergency. “Each day these flats are left empty is another missed opportunity to support the many thousands of Rochdalians living in temporary or unsuitable accommodation. “The council and GMCA have confirmed their commitment to resolving this longstanding and emotive issue, and I will continue to work with colleagues across government to ensure the best quality housing in Rochdale is realised.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh Hannah Fleming, Director of Regeneration and Asset Improvement at Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, said: “It’s important that we make the right decision on the future of College Bank. “Our focus throughout has been on doing the right thing for current and future customers, ensuring we can provide safe, warm, affordable homes that meet housing need for generations to come. “Future regeneration options are still being discussed with our partners, including Rochdale Council and the Mayor of Greater Manchester. No final decision has yet been made by the RBH Board. “What we do know is that there are no simple options. The buildings are more than 60 years old and have continued to deteriorate. Keeping them would require very major works requiring customers to move out for at least a decade. “That is why, in October, 2025, the board made the difficult decision to begin rehousing customers while longer-term plans are considered. This decision was taken because of concerns about the long-term condition and safety of the buildings, and not because any final regeneration decision had been reached. “We have already made significant progress on the rehousing programme, with just under 90 households left to find their new home and most customers already settled in their new homes. “We are working individually with each household to ensure their move is as simple and straightforward as it possibly can be.” The mayor’s office has been approached for a comment. articles.title: Heywood and Middleton North MP visits Redwood School’s sixth form at Phoenix Centre
articles.excerpt: Elsie Blundell, MP for Heywood and Middleton North, visited Redwood School’s sixth form at the Phoenix Centre to engage with students and staff about their educational initiatives.
articles.content_html:
Elsie Blundell, the Member of Parliament for Heywood and Middleton North, visited the Redwood School’s sixth form campus located at the Phoenix Centre in Heywood on October 15. During her visit, she interacted with learners and staff to understand their efforts in supporting young people with special educational needs and disabilities.

Ms Blundell praised the teaching team for their role in helping students build essential skills and confidence for education, adult life, and future employment.

She expressed her pride in having such a facility within her constituency, stating, "I’m so proud to have this facility - and the learners and parents - in my constituency."

The visit included discussions about various lessons, including the importance of recycling. Ms Blundell also enjoyed a meal of soup during her time at the school, which she described as "delicious." She thanked the staff and students for their warm welcome and the valuable lessons shared during her visit.

In her reflections on the day, Ms Blundell commended the young people, parents, teachers, and support staff for their hard work, writing, "Well done again to the young people, parents, teachers and support staff."

This visit highlights the ongoing commitment to enhancing educational opportunities for students with special needs in the Heywood area.

articles.title: College Bank’s future remains a housing question as residents move from the Seven Sisters
articles.excerpt: College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.
articles.content_html:
College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.

That is evidence of rehousing progress at a particular date, not evidence that replacement homes have been constructed or that a final demolition or refurbishment programme is approved. Earlier reporting described continuing uncertainty over the solution for the Seven Sisters.

RBH says resident safety drives the move and that it is supporting tenants through the process. A complete account should include the position of residents who wish to stay, the available alternatives and any future right-to-return arrangements.

This is separate from the neighbouring Lower Falinge proposal. Combining the two without checking their boundaries and replacement totals risks overstating supply and obscuring the number of existing affordable homes temporarily or permanently lost.

The January 2026 regulator judgement recognises RBH’s governance improvement but identifies material risks around investment and regeneration. It is not a project approval or an assessment of whether demolition is the best option.

Until the final scheme is evidenced, its contribution to the housing target is unknown. The practical questions are the cost, safety and quality of the eventual homes, and whether existing residents benefit from the change.

Location: College Bank / Seven Sisters, Rochdale

Planning stage: Rehousing underway; a verified final replacement or refurbishment scheme not established

Homes: No reliable new-home total established for a final future scheme

Let or for sale: Existing social housing; future tenure and costs require a confirmed scheme

Land: Existing urban residential land

Final planning agreement: No final replacement/refurbishment scheme, permission or executed development agreement was established from the reviewed records.

Exact rents / prices: Exact future rents, service charges and any guaranteed return-tenancy costs cannot be reported without a confirmed scheme and terms. They are not provided in the public update reviewed.

Affordable breakdown: Existing social housing; final retained, demolished and replacement totals, tenure and net gain are not established.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded capacity established. A final scheme and net household change are needed before assessing additional school demand.

Funded healthcare capacity: No final scheme-specific funded NHS capacity established; rehousing progress does not measure GP capacity.

Funded transport capacity: No final funded transport-capacity package established. Existing town-centre access is not evidence of additional service provision.

articles.title: Hollingworth Road’s 309 homes: the school land promise needs a delivery explanation
articles.excerpt: Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.
articles.content_html:
Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.

Pre-decision reporting identifies 47 affordable homes, approximately 15.2% of the scheme. However, its quoted breakdown of 12 social-rent and 25 shared-ownership homes totals only 37. The missing ten must be reconciled against the final affordable schedule before a complete tenure split is published.

The school requires careful explanation. Reporting on the planning assessment says population projections did not then justify immediate delivery. Reserving school land is therefore different from promising that a school will open alongside the first houses. The decision must explain funding, demand thresholds and interim provision.

More than 1,000 objections were reported, including concerns about infrastructure. Bloor identifies transport assessments, drainage measures and replacement visitor parking, but the final conditions and funded works determine what will actually be delivered.

Bloor joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Location: Hollingworth Road / north of Smithy Bridge, Littleborough

Planning stage: Council June 2026 update records site-preparation work

Homes: 309 revised scheme homes; earlier proposal was 312

Let or for sale: 47 affordable homes reported; social rent/shared ownership envisaged; complete split not reconciled

Land: Farmland / greenfield in an allocated former Green Belt location

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: Bloor’s live Hollingworth Rise page advertises plot 271, a three-bedroom Kane, at £334,995; plot 278, a four-bedroom Locke, at £449,995; and plot 267, a four-bedroom Watercroft, at £489,995. These are market asking prices. Exact social rents and shared-ownership shares, rents and charges are not provided in the reviewed records.

Affordable breakdown: 47 affordable homes reported, comprising 26 two-bedroom, 17 three-bedroom and four four-bedroom dwellings. Published tenure reporting gives 12 social-rent plus 25 shared-ownership homes, only 37: the other ten remain unreconciled. Do not silently change the figures.

Funded school capacity: Land for a potential 420-place primary school is identified. The planning assessment reported no immediate need; an allocated plot is not a funded building. A confirmed budget, operator, demand trigger and opening date were not established.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Drainage, active travel and visitor-parking changes are proposed. Reported contributions exceeding £3 million are not a verified executed item-by-item transport budget, payment record or service-capacity increase.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Rochdale October half-term 2026: school dates and free family activities
articles.excerpt: The council's recommended half-term runs from 26 to 30 October. Here are verified free activities at Rochdale Town Hall, Wardle Library and local family hubs, plus what parents should check before travelling.
articles.content_html:
Families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow can start planning the October school break, with the council recommending Monday 26 to Friday 30 October 2026 as the autumn half-term holiday. The dates are a borough-wide recommended pattern, rather than a guarantee for every school, so parents should check their own school's calendar before booking childcare or a trip.

One of the clearest free options announced so far is at Rochdale Town Hall. Its Spooktacular Half Term programme is advertised for every day from Monday 26 October to Sunday 1 November, running from 10am to 4pm at the Town Hall on The Esplanade, OL16 1AZ. The organiser describes family-friendly Halloween activities, with free entry and no advance booking required. More detailed individual activities have not yet all been listed, so it is worth checking the official Town Hall event information before travelling.

For families wanting a short outing at the end of the break, Wardle Library's Kids' Club is listed in the council's October events calendar for Saturday 31 October. The free session runs from 10am until 12.30pm at 448 Birch Road, Wardle, OL12 9LH. It is aimed at families with children aged four and over and normally includes crafts, activities and challenges. The council says there is no need to book.

Parents and carers with younger children also have the borough's family hubs to investigate. Council information lists activities for children aged up to five at locations including Heybrook, Howard Street, Meanwood, Castleton, Deeplish and Sandbrook, as well as centres in Middleton, Heywood, Littleborough and the wider Pennines area. The council describes these activities as free unless otherwise stated. The listing is a directory rather than a confirmed half-term timetable, so families should consult their nearest hub's current programme instead of assuming ordinary weekly sessions continue during the holiday.

Not every regular children's library session runs during school holidays. Some Bookstart activities are explicitly described as term-time sessions, making it especially important to check dates rather than turn up on the strength of a weekly listing.

Parents trying to keep costs down can therefore rely on the confirmed free Town Hall programme and check the Wardle Library listing, while using the council's event directory to see whether anything else is added nearer the time. This guide covers confirmed information available on 13 October; opening arrangements and individual sessions may change.

articles.title: Rochdale Sixth Form College students disciplined for ranking looks in controversial online group
articles.excerpt: Students at Rochdale Sixth Form College have faced disciplinary action after creating a Microsoft Teams group that encouraged members to rank their physical attractiveness, with rules enforced by a self-styled 'Founding Father'.
articles.content_html:
Students at Rochdale Sixth Form College have been disciplined following the establishment of a Microsoft Teams group that instructed members to categorise themselves based on physical attractiveness.

The group, named 'Rochdale Sixth Form College BP Club', used terminology associated with online incel and manosphere communities, with 'BP' standing for 'black pill'.

The organiser of the group, who referred to himself as the 'Founding Father', mandated that members assign themselves to categories labelled 'Chad', 'HTN' (high-tier normie), and 'LTN' (low-tier normie), which ranked individuals from exceptionally attractive to above or below average.

Members were warned of 'serious consequences' for failing to adhere to the group's rules, which included using 'formal language' in their communications.

Messages exchanged within the group included inappropriate comments about other students, as well as profanity and demands to expand the group to 100 members.

The organiser also issued strikes to members who did not comply with the established rules, further enforcing a culture of ranking and judgement based on looks.

The disciplinary actions taken by the college reflect a broader concern regarding the impact of such online communities on student wellbeing and the promotion of harmful ideologies.

The college has not publicly detailed the specific consequences faced by the students involved, but the incident raises important questions about the influence of social media and peer pressure in educational environments.

articles.title: The children left waiting: has Rochdale cleared its 1,400-case SEND backlog?
articles.excerpt: After an Ombudsman identified more than 1,400 delayed SEND review decisions, Rochdale Council challenged the figures and reported improvements. Have affected families received the support they were owed?
articles.content_html:
For parents raising a child with special educational needs, an Education, Health and Care (EHC) plan is far more than paperwork. It sets out the provision a council must secure, and can determine the specialist teaching, therapies and support a child receives. When it is not reviewed or amended on time, families can be left uncertain about whether their child's needs are being met and when they can challenge decisions.

In March 2025 the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman publicised an investigation identifying widespread delays in Rochdale Borough Council's handling of annual reviews. The council later disputed the number reported, while also reporting substantial improvements to its service. More than 18 months after the public findings, a critical question remains: can the council demonstrate that the historic cases have been resolved and that any lost provision has been addressed?

WHAT THE OMBUDSMAN FOUND

The Ombudsman's report, decision reference 24 010 066 dated 10 February 2025, followed concerns about delayed updates to children's EHC plans. It found fault in the council's delays sending decisions after annual reviews and in issuing amended plans.

According to the Ombudsman's March 2025 account, the council had more than 1,400 cases in which it had failed to tell parents within four weeks whether an EHC plan would be amended, maintained or ceased. In 600 cases the council had decided to maintain or cease plans, leaving families waiting longer than they should have to exercise potential appeal rights. Among 300 cases where the council decided to amend a plan, nearly 100 children and young people were still waiting for a draft plan after six months.

The number of completed reviews for which updated EHC plans had not been issued rose from more than 800 in June 2024 to more than 1,300 by October 2024. These figures represent different stages of the process; they must not be added together or treated as proof that every child lost education. They nevertheless show the scale of missed statutory timescales.

THE COUNCIL CHALLENGED THE 1,447 FIGURE

The council's own account subsequently differed sharply from the headline number. Minutes of the Health, Schools and Care Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 23 July 2025 record the Head of SEND saying a misinterpretation of data by the Ombudsman had led to an incorrect report of 1,447 overdue reviews. Councillors were told there had been 808 overdue reviews as of December 2024.

The same minutes recorded the council's position that 75% of its annual-review outcomes had been communicated within four weeks in 2024, compared with a national figure of 44.4%. The council said an improvement action plan had been implemented in May 2025 and was reviewed monthly.

There may be differences in the dates, definitions or stages of cases counted in the two figures. The published minutes do not reconcile them in detail, and they do not by themselves overturn the Ombudsman's formal findings. Families deserve a clear explanation of precisely what each total counted.

IMPROVEMENTS REPORTED — BUT DID THE OLDEST CASES CLOSE?

The council's December 2025 portfolio reporting provided evidence of progress. It recorded that 96% of annual reviews were receiving responses within four weeks in the latest reported quarter, compared with 63% previously. The council said it had 3,704 active EHC plans in November 2025 and separately reported completion of its Ombudsman annual-review improvement action plan.

Those are significant improvements, but a high rate of new decisions made on time is not necessarily the same as clearing the older backlog. The reports reviewed for this investigation do not establish, as at 12 October 2026, exactly how many cases identified during the original Ombudsman investigation remained unresolved, nor the length of any remaining delays.

A FURTHER UPHELD COMPLAINT

An Ombudsman decision dated 25 June 2026 illustrates what prolonged delays can mean to an individual family. In case 25 004 481, a child's EHC plan had been reviewed in May 2024 and should have been amended by August 2024. The final amended plan was not issued until August 2025, around 12 months late.

The child had been permanently excluded from school in January 2025. Although the council arranged a place at a pupil referral unit, the Ombudsman found that it had failed to retain adequate oversight of whether the alternative arrangements met the child's needs. It also found poor communication and complaint handling. The decision recorded that the council apologised and offered a financial remedy.

This decision, published in June 2026, largely concerned events during 2024 and 2025. It should not be presented as proof that the original backlog persisted at the same level in June 2026. It does, however, show the practical consequences that can follow when plans and provision are not kept under proper review.

HAVE FAMILIES BEEN REMEDIED FOR LOST SUPPORT?

In another upheld case, decision 23 009 491 dated 30 September 2024, the Ombudsman found Rochdale had failed to amend a young person's plan after a December 2021 review, failed to complete subsequent reviews and failed to secure specified special educational provision. Remedies included payments for missed provision.

The existence of individual remedies raises a wider public-interest question: did the council assess other children affected by the systemic delays to determine whether education, therapies, specialist provision or opportunities to appeal had been lost? The original backlog figure cannot be used as a count of children who missed schooling, and no such figure is established by the records examined here.

ROCHDALE DAILY ASKS THE COUNCIL TO RESPOND

On 12 October 2026, Rochdale Daily emailed the council's published Corporate Policy, Performance and Improvement address and asked for the questions to be passed to its SEND service and Media Office. The council has been invited to comment on three key points:

First, why do the public records contain figures of 1,447 and 808 overdue reviews, and can the council reconcile the measures, definitions and dates behind them?

Second, what are the latest verified figures for outstanding EHC annual-review decisions and amended plans as of October 2026, including cases beyond statutory deadlines and the oldest unresolved cases? How many of those identified in the original Ombudsman report have been completed?

Third, has the council assessed whether families affected by delayed plans missed educational provision, therapy, specialist support or appeal opportunities; how many cases were assessed; and how many families received redress or compensation, and of what total value?

The council has also been asked what improvements have followed the completed action plan. This invitation is open. Any substantive response will be reported fairly and the article updated. No response had been received by the time this report was prepared; the questions were sent on the evening of 12 October.

The issue is not only whether Rochdale completed an action plan. It is whether the children and young people whose reviews were delayed received the support they were legally entitled to, and whether families have been told what happened to their cases.

HELP FOR AFFECTED FAMILIES

Rochdale Council's confidential SEND Advice Line can be reached on 0300 303 0380 or at SENDAdviceLine@Rochdale.Gov.UK. Barnardo's Rochdale SENDIASS provides free impartial advice on EHC plans, annual reviews and appeals on 01706 769634, or via rochdale.sendiass@barnardos.org.uk. Parents should keep copies of their annual-review paperwork, dates and correspondence, and seek independent advice promptly because appeal deadlines can be short.

Rochdale Daily welcomes confidential accounts from families affected by delayed SEND support at news@rochdaledaily.co.uk. Please do not send sensitive information about a child until a secure method of sharing it has been agreed.

articles.title: Mayor Faisal Rana visits Rochdale Sixth Form College to see student support and results
articles.excerpt: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, highlighting its student support, pastoral provision and recent academic achievements.
articles.content_html: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress have visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, meeting Principal Karl Smith and touring the college to see its facilities and student support. The visit included the Achievement Centre, which provides additional support for students who may be falling behind or need extra help with their studies. The Mayor and Mayoress also visited the student café and highlighted the college's focus on pastoral support, attendance and punctuality. ### College results and progression Rochdale Sixth Form College says its students achieved strong results in 2026. The college's website describes it as one of the country's strongest sixth form colleges for student progress, while its latest results announcement reported exceptional A-level and BTEC outcomes. The college also says around 80% of its students progress to higher education and that it has retained an Outstanding Ofsted judgement. The college's website currently highlights students progressing to Oxford and Cambridge, including former Oulder Hill student Joseph, who achieved three A*s and an A* in his EPQ before progressing to Cambridge, and former Hollingworth student Summer, who achieved four A*s and an A* in her EPQ before progressing to Oxford. Faisal Rana said the visit was particularly meaningful because four of his children had attended the college and achieved what he described as exceptional results. He said the visit offered a different perspective on the college, beyond that of a parent. He also praised the college's emphasis on supporting students, raising aspirations and creating opportunities for young people in the borough. Principal Karl Smith hosted the visit. Students across Rochdale have been opening their A-Level results today, bringing two years of study, examinations and anxious waiting to an end as young people discover whether they have secured university places, apprenticeships or their next step into employment.

Results day on Thursday 13 August comes during another strong year nationally. Across the UK, 28.5% of A-Level entries were awarded an A* or A, while in England the figure was 28.3%. More than 262,000 UK 18-year-olds had been accepted onto university courses by results day.

In the North West, 26.5% of A-Level entries received an A* or A in 2026, compared with 26.6% in 2025 and 23.5% in 2019. The figures continue to show a substantial regional divide, with London recording 32.7% of entries at A* or A this year.

For Rochdale, particular attention falls on Rochdale Sixth Form College, which has developed a strong academic record since opening in September 2010. The college was created following longstanding concerns about post-16 attainment in the borough and the number of local students travelling outside Rochdale for sixth-form education.

The college's early results quickly attracted national attention. It was ranked second among sixth form colleges for value added in Department for Education performance tables in 2013 and later achieved first place for A-Level progress for several consecutive years. By January 2019 it had been ranked first in Department for Education performance tables for five years running, and in 2021 it won Sixth Form College of the Year at the Tes FE Awards.

More recent government performance data has continued to show strong progress. Department for Education figures for 2024 recorded an average A-Level result of B- at Rochdale Sixth Form College and an A-Level progress score of +0.41, classified as well above average. The 2025 figures again recorded an average result of B-, with an average point score of 37.33 and a progress measure of +0.48, also classified as well above average.

The historical picture matters because Rochdale Sixth Form College was established in part to tackle a period in which the borough's A-Level performance had lagged behind national averages. Its subsequent performance provides a significant contrast with the concerns that led to the college being established more than 15 years ago.

Today's results are also notable politically because Rochdale's MP, Paul Waugh, has recently joined the Department for Education. Mr Waugh was appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education in July 2026, giving Rochdale a direct connection to national education policy.

Today's A-Level cohort completed almost all of its education before Mr Waugh entered the department, so the 2026 results cannot reasonably be attributed to his tenure. Future results, however, will increasingly provide part of the national record against which the Government's education policies — and the ministers responsible for them — are judged.

That will be particularly relevant in areas such as Rochdale because regional inequality remains one of the clearest challenges facing education ministers. This year's figures show 32.7% of A-Level entries in London receiving A* or A, compared with 26.5% in the North West and 23.1% in both the North East and East Midlands.

For students receiving their results today, however, national statistics and ministerial records are unlikely to be the immediate priority. For some, the results will confirm university places they have worked towards for years. Others will move into apprenticeships, employment or further study, while students who have missed required grades can consider Clearing and alternative routes.

Whatever the individual results, today marks the end of one chapter for Rochdale's students and the beginning of another.

articles.title: Summer makeover under way at St Mary’s CE Primary School in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: St Mary’s CE Primary School in Rochdale is undergoing a summer makeover, with improvement works taking place in the school hall and reception classroom ahead of the new term.
articles.content_html:
St Mary’s CE Primary School in Rochdale is a hive of activity this summer as improvement works continue across key areas of the school ahead of pupils returning in September.

Watergrove Trust says both the school hall and reception classroom are being given a makeover during the summer break, including the installation of new ceilings and acoustic baffles.

The works are designed to refresh the learning environment and improve the spaces used by pupils, staff and the wider school community.

The Trust said: “It’s all happening at St. Mary’s CE Primary School, Rochdale this summer; a real hive of activity as the hall and reception class are both having a makeover including new ceilings and acoustic baffles.

“We can’t wait to see the finished spaces in September as we continue to provide more for our community.”

St Mary’s CE Primary School has served the Rochdale community for more than 150 years and is part of the Watergrove Trust, which brings together schools across the borough with a shared focus on school improvement and community provision.

The latest summer works continue that investment, with the refurbished spaces expected to be ready for the start of the new academic year in September.

articles.title: Every secondary school in Rochdale ranked: GCSEs, behaviour, attendance, Ofsted and what happens after Year 11
articles.excerpt: A parent's guide to the borough's 13 mainstream secondary schools - looking beyond GCSE league tables to behaviour, destinations, SEND provision, pastoral support and enrichment.
articles.content_html:
Choosing a secondary school is one of the biggest decisions a parent makes.

But deciding which school is "best" is considerably more complicated than looking at a GCSE league table.

A school could achieve excellent examination results while struggling with attendance. Another might have lower attainment but exceptional pastoral support, SEND provision and behaviour. A third might excel at getting pupils into college, apprenticeships or employment.

So Rochdale Daily has taken a broader look.

We have examined the latest publicly available information for the 13 mainstream secondary schools listed by Rochdale Borough Council, considering: Attainment 8; grade 5+ in English and mathematics; EBacc participation and performance; post-16 destinations; attendance; suspensions and behaviour; Ofsted findings; pastoral support; SEND provision; personal development; and extra-curricular opportunities.

The result is intended as a parent's guide rather than an official government league table.

There is also an important gap in the national data.

Why there is no Progress 8 score this year

Progress 8 would ordinarily be one of the most useful measures because it asks how much progress pupils make between primary school and GCSEs rather than simply how high their final grades are.

But the Department for Education cannot calculate Progress 8 for either 2024/25 or 2025/26 because pupils in those cohorts did not have the necessary Key Stage 2 assessment baseline following Covid disruption.

That means this year's Attainment 8 figures measure where pupils finished — not how far the school moved them from their starting point. That distinction matters.

Nationally, state-school pupils achieved an average Attainment 8 score of 46, while 45.4% achieved grade 5 or better in both English and mathematics. Across Rochdale, those figures were 40.6 and 35% respectively.

1. Hollingworth Academy, Milnrow — best academic performer

Hollingworth sits at the top primarily because its latest examination performance is significantly ahead of the Rochdale average. Its 2025 figures show an Attainment 8 score of 51.1, with 59.8% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths and an EBacc average point score of 4.48.

That means Hollingworth's Attainment 8 score was more than 10 points above the Rochdale average of 40.6 and also above the national state-school average of 46. The school's own 2025 figures similarly report an Attainment 8 score of around 51 and 60% achieving strong passes in English and maths.

There is, however, an interesting weakness. Only 22.2% entered the EBacc, compared with 40.5% nationally. And its published destination data for the 2023 leavers shows 84% of disadvantaged pupils continuing in education, apprenticeship or employment, compared with 94% of non-disadvantaged pupils nationally.

So although Hollingworth comfortably leads academically, parents should not interpret first place as meaning it dominates every measure.

Strengths: GCSE attainment, English and mathematics, broad academic performance. Watch: EBacc entry and destination gap among disadvantaged pupils.

2. Oulder Hill Leadership Academy — strongest all-round improvement story

Oulder Hill deserves to be near the top because the picture today is substantially different from that of its predecessor school. Its latest 2025 data gives an Attainment 8 score of 44.4, with 46.2% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths — the latter above both the Rochdale average and around the national level.

The more important finding comes from Ofsted. Following its January 2025 inspection, inspectors judged the quality of education, behaviour and attitudes, personal development, and leadership and management all Good.

That's particularly significant because the predecessor Oulder Hill Community School had previously been judged Inadequate before conversion to the Star Academies trust. Ofsted also confirmed that the school meets requirements for giving pupils access to information about technical education and apprenticeships.

Oulder Hill therefore performs particularly well in this ranking because it combines respectable attainment with strong independent inspection findings on behaviour, personal development and leadership.

Strengths: Behaviour, personal development, improving academic results, careers provision. Watch: Academic attainment remains below the national Attainment 8 average.

3. Wardle Academy — strong pastoral and academic balance

Wardle's 2025 Attainment 8 score was 44.1, above Rochdale's 40.6 average although still just below England's 46. Around 39.1% achieved grade 5+ in English and mathematics, also above the Rochdale borough figure of 35%.

But Wardle gets additional credit because the evidence isn't purely academic. The school was rated Good at its most recent Ofsted inspection, with inspectors reporting that pupils feel safe and happy and highlighting the strong relationships between pupils and staff and the school's pastoral approach.

Wardle also has specialist resourced SEND provision, something that may matter far more than league-table position for families of children with additional needs.

Strengths: Good Ofsted judgement, pastoral support, SEND provision, above-borough academic attainment. Watch: Results are solid rather than exceptional nationally.

4. St Cuthbert's RC High School — outstanding post-school destination performance

St Cuthbert's latest published results show an Attainment 8 score of 39.66, with 27.31% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 19% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.36. Those academic results place the school below Rochdale's overall averages.

But one number changes the picture considerably. The school reports 93.69% of pupils staying in education or entering employment after Key Stage 4.

That is precisely why simply ranking schools by GCSEs can mislead parents. St Cuthbert's examination figures are not among the borough's strongest, yet almost 94% of its leavers are progressing onwards.

Strengths: Post-16 destinations. Watch: GCSE attainment and strong passes in English and mathematics.

5. Cardinal Langley RC High School, Middleton — excellent destinations despite weaker 2025 attainment

Cardinal Langley's latest published government figures show an Attainment 8 score of 40.9, with 31.8% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 29.5% EBacc entry, an EBacc average point score of 3.46 — and 94% of leavers progressing to education, employment or an apprenticeship.

That 94% destination figure is excellent. The academic picture is more mixed: Attainment 8 is around the Rochdale average while English and mathematics strong passes remain below both borough and national levels.

Its position therefore reflects a strong record of getting pupils into their next destination even where the latest GCSE headline statistics are less remarkable.

Strengths: Destinations, post-16 progression. Watch: English and mathematics attainment.

6. Holy Family RC & CE College, Heywood — strong ethos and pastoral environment

Holy Family is particularly difficult to judge solely through a numerical league table because some of the most compelling evidence concerns school culture. Its most recent established Ofsted judgement is Good, while its denominational inspection rated the college Outstanding.

The school describes itself as an oversubscribed joint Roman Catholic and Church of England college and places a particularly strong emphasis on pastoral care, personal development and Christian ethos. For parents prioritising school environment alongside results, Holy Family deserves to sit toward the upper half of the table.

Strengths: Pastoral environment, ethos, inspection record. Watch: Parents should compare the latest individual GCSE subject outcomes when making an academic comparison with the schools above.

7. Dixons Middleton Academy — middle of the pack academically, Good Ofsted

Dixons Middleton recorded an Attainment 8 score of 40.3, with 33.6% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 42.9% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.57.

The EBacc entry rate is notable because it exceeds the Rochdale borough average and is around the national level. The school is rated Good by Ofsted, and its latest published destinations data indicates approximately 90% continuing into education, employment or apprenticeships.

The wider picture isn't perfect. Historical Parent View data collected around the 2024 inspection showed considerable disagreement among parents over behaviour and communication, although Parent View samples are voluntary and should never be treated like a representative opinion poll.

Strengths: EBacc participation, Good Ofsted judgement. Watch: Overall attainment and English/maths strong passes.

8. Falinge Park High School — around borough average with notable challenges

Government data for the predecessor establishment recorded an Attainment 8 score of 40.5, with 36.1% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 24.8% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.37. Those figures are remarkably close to Rochdale's overall results.

But Falinge serves a particularly challenging intake. Among disadvantaged pupils, Attainment 8 was 36.6, while 30.3% achieved strong passes in English and mathematics.

Interestingly, pupils with English as an additional language actually outperformed the school's overall cohort on several measures: EAL pupils recorded an Attainment 8 score of 42.6 compared with 40.5 overall. That is an important achievement which a simplistic league table would completely miss.

The school has since converted to academy status, meaning some current government tables show no comparable data under the new establishment record.

Strengths: Outcomes for EAL pupils. Watch: Overall attainment and disadvantaged-pupil gap.

9. Newhouse Academy, Heywood — behaviour stronger than academic outcomes

Newhouse recorded an Attainment 8 score of 38.9, with 29.7% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 30.8% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.26. That places academic performance below both Rochdale and national averages.

Its Ofsted picture is more encouraging. Although its 2023 inspection resulted in Requires Improvement overall, inspectors judged behaviour and attitudes, personal development, and leadership and management all Good. The school also underwent a monitoring visit in June 2025.

Newhouse has a substantial pastoral and attendance operation, including dedicated pastoral managers and an education welfare officer, with pupils' attendance monitored weekly. This is therefore another school where the headline GCSE statistics don't tell the full story.

Strengths: Behaviour, personal development, pastoral and attendance infrastructure. Watch: Academic attainment remains below borough averages.

10. Matthew Moss High School — academic outcomes currently below borough average

Matthew Moss recorded an Attainment 8 score of 39.3, with 34.3% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 26% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.37. These figures put the school slightly below Rochdale's overall attainment measures.

Its disadvantaged cohort recorded an Attainment 8 score of 34.7, with 27.5% obtaining grade 5+ in English and mathematics.

The gender difference is also substantial: girls achieved an Attainment 8 score of 42.3, compared with 36 for boys. That is potentially one of the more interesting findings in the borough and deserves further investigation.

Strengths: Some stronger performance among girls and EAL pupils. Watch: Overall attainment and attainment among disadvantaged pupils and boys.

11. Kingsway Park High School — results weak, enrichment exceptionally interesting

On GCSE figures alone, Kingsway Park would sit near the bottom. Latest government figures show an Attainment 8 score of 35.3, with around 18% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 18.7% EBacc entry, an EBacc average point score of 2.87 — and 91% progressing to a recognised destination.

But Kingsway Park is perhaps the clearest demonstration of why this ranking goes beyond GCSE results. The school has developed an unusually extensive enrichment programme aimed particularly at children living in poverty, with reported activities including Brazilian jiu-jitsu, football, boxing, lacrosse, windsurfing, theatre, free music tuition and instruments for pupils. The school has also operated practical support including a food bank and assistance for families experiencing hardship.

Headteacher Simon Ward has spoken openly about tackling behaviour problems and attempting to provide opportunities pupils might otherwise never experience.

That does not erase weak examination performance. But it means describing Kingsway Park simply as one of Rochdale's "worst schools" would be unfair and potentially meaningless to a parent whose priority is enrichment, belonging or pastoral support.

Strengths: Enrichment, pastoral intervention, opportunities for disadvantaged children. Watch: GCSE attainment remains substantially below borough and national levels.

12. St Anne's CE Academy, Middleton — strong personal-development offer but academic comparison remains difficult

St Anne's was judged Good across all criteria by Ofsted in 2024. The academy describes a broad programme of extra-curricular activities alongside updated science and IT facilities and a nurturing Christian environment open to pupils of all faiths and backgrounds. This gives it a stronger qualitative picture than a purely exam-based comparison might suggest.

Strengths: Ofsted, enrichment, personal development and ethos. Watch: Comparable current GCSE data should be considered alongside the qualitative strengths before parents make a decision.

Edgar Wood Academy — not fairly rankable yet

Edgar Wood deserves a separate category. It is a relatively new school and the 2025 government performance tables show no Key Stage 4 cohort available for meaningful comparison. Trying to put it 13th simply because GCSE data doesn't exist would therefore be ridiculous.

The important evidence instead comes from Ofsted. The academy was inspected again in June 2026, following an earlier monitoring visit in May 2025. Because it is still developing and only recently reached the point at which older pupils move through the school, Rochdale Daily considers it unranked rather than last. That distinction matters.

What the league table tells us

There isn't actually one "best school" for every child.

If GCSE results are your priority, Hollingworth Academy is currently the clear standout: its 51.1 Attainment 8 score and approximately 60% strong-pass rate in English and mathematics are comfortably ahead of the borough averages.

If behaviour and personal development matter, Oulder Hill, Wardle, Newhouse and St Anne's have particularly useful independent inspection evidence.

If SEND provision is critical, parents should look beyond league tables altogether. Wardle, for example, has dedicated resourced provision. SEND arrangements differ significantly between schools and between individual children's needs.

If destinations matter, St Cuthbert's and Cardinal Langley both report approximately 94% progressing into education, employment or other recognised destinations.

If extracurricular opportunity matters, Kingsway Park's enrichment offer stands out despite comparatively weak academic figures.

And what about attendance and suspensions?

These deserve particular attention. Across Rochdale as a whole, secondary-school suspension levels have been sufficiently high to warrant concern, but using borough-wide numbers to label an individual school would be unfair.

Suspensions can also be counter-intuitive. A school recording more suspensions may genuinely have worse behaviour. But it may instead have a stricter behaviour policy and suspend pupils for conduct another school manages internally. Likewise, low suspensions don't automatically prove excellent behaviour.

That is why Rochdale Daily considers suspension data alongside Ofsted's behaviour and attitudes judgement, attendance, persistent absence and other evidence rather than awarding points simply for having fewer suspensions.

Attendance has similar complications. Schools serving communities experiencing severe deprivation, unstable housing, chronic illness or high levels of additional need can face greater attendance problems that are not entirely within the school's control. It remains an important measure — but it requires context.

Rochdale remains behind nationally on attainment

The wider borough picture shouldn't be ignored. Across Rochdale, the averages are: Attainment 8, 40.6; grade 5+ English and maths, 35%; EBacc entry, 30.2%; EBacc average point score, 3.47. National state-school figures are: Attainment 8, 46; grade 5+ English and maths, 45.4%; EBacc entry, 40.5%; EBacc average point score, 4.09.

So although individual schools are doing exceptionally well, Rochdale as a borough continues to have a substantial secondary-attainment gap with England overall. That is arguably the biggest education story of all.

Rochdale Daily's overall guide

1. Hollingworth Academy — strongest academics. 2. Oulder Hill Leadership Academy — strongest recent all-round inspection picture. 3. Wardle Academy — strong academic/pastoral balance. 4. St Cuthbert's RC High School — excellent destinations. 5. Cardinal Langley RC High School — strong destinations. 6. Holy Family RC & CE College — strong ethos and pastoral environment. 7. Dixons Middleton Academy — solid all-round performer. 8. Falinge Park High School — around borough average, noteworthy EAL outcomes. 9. Newhouse Academy — improving with good behaviour and personal development findings. 10. Matthew Moss High School — below-average current attainment. 11. Kingsway Park High School — weak attainment but exceptional enrichment story. 12. St Anne's CE Academy — Good inspection and broad enrichment; insufficient comparable attainment evidence for a higher position. Unranked: Edgar Wood Academy — too new for a fair full academic comparison.

A word to parents

A league table should be the beginning of choosing a school, not the end.

A child with SEND may thrive somewhere completely different from the highest-scoring GCSE school. A child struggling emotionally may benefit more from exceptional pastoral support. An academically driven pupil may be better suited to a school with particularly strong examination outcomes and curriculum breadth. A child who needs confidence may flourish because of sport, music, drama or enrichment.

Parents should therefore look at results, behaviour, attendance, pastoral care, SEND provision, destinations, enrichment — and how their own child feels inside the school. That gives a much more meaningful picture than a GCSE percentage alone.

Sources and methodology: Rochdale Daily's analysis uses the Department for Education's 2025 school performance tables, latest available Ofsted inspections and monitoring visits, Rochdale Borough Council's official secondary-school list, schools' statutory published information and publicly available destination, SEND, pastoral and enrichment information. Where directly comparable current information was unavailable, this is stated rather than estimated. Progress 8 has deliberately not been used for 2025 because the Department for Education says it cannot be calculated for the current cohorts due to the absence of Key Stage 2 baseline assessments following Covid disruption.

articles.title: GCSE results day 2026: What Rochdale parents need to know – and why one set of grades doesn't define a future
articles.excerpt: From college offers to apprenticeships and changing employer expectations, here's everything Rochdale parents need to know before GCSE results day.
articles.content_html:
Thousands of teenagers across Rochdale borough will soon collect one of the most important envelopes of their young lives as GCSE results day approaches.

For many families, results day brings a mixture of excitement, nerves and uncertainty. Parents naturally want the best for their children, but education experts say GCSEs are increasingly becoming just one of several routes into higher education, apprenticeships and long-term careers rather than the single deciding factor they were once perceived to be.

This year's GCSE results will be released on Thursday 20 August, with schools across Rochdale opening to allow students to collect their grades and speak with teachers about their next steps. Students will receive provisional results before certificates are issued later in the year.

For many teenagers, the next destination has already been decided through conditional offers from sixth forms and colleges. Most colleges will honour offers provided students meet the required grades, while admissions teams are usually available on results day to discuss alternatives if results are different from those expected.

Compared with a decade ago, today's post-16 education landscape is far more flexible. Alongside traditional A Levels, students can now choose from T Levels, vocational qualifications, apprenticeships and technical training, giving young people far more options depending on their interests and career ambitions. Greater Manchester has also continued expanding the Greater Manchester Baccalaureate (MBacc), designed to place technical education on an equal footing with academic study while creating clearer pathways into local industries.

Parents often ask whether GCSEs still matter.

The answer is yes—but perhaps not in the way they once did.

GCSEs remain important because they open doors. Most sixth forms, colleges, universities and apprenticeship providers require passes in English Language and Mathematics, while many A Level courses ask for a minimum grade in the subject students wish to study. Employers also continue to value GCSEs as evidence of literacy, numeracy and commitment, particularly when recruiting school leavers with little previous work experience. Ofqual has described GCSEs as a 'passport to opportunity', providing access to further education, apprenticeships and employment.

However, the employment market has changed dramatically. Increasingly, recruiters say experience, practical skills, communication, teamwork and attitude become far more important than GCSE grades as careers progress.

Recruitment specialists consistently report that while GCSEs may be used as an initial screening tool for younger applicants, employers recruiting experienced candidates are far more interested in work history, achievements, technical skills and professional qualifications. In sectors such as construction, logistics, digital technology, engineering, health and social care, apprenticeships have become an increasingly respected route into well-paid careers.

That does not mean students should dismiss their exams. Strong GCSE results can provide greater choice and flexibility, particularly for competitive sixth forms, universities and professional careers such as medicine, dentistry and law. But equally, disappointing grades do not prevent someone building a successful future.

Parents are also encouraged to remember that results day is only one moment in a much longer journey. Colleges regularly help students who narrowly miss entry requirements by suggesting alternative courses, foundation programmes or vocational pathways that still lead towards the same career goals.

For students who do not achieve the grade 4 pass in English or Mathematics, the law requires them to continue studying those subjects alongside most post-16 courses until they achieve the qualification or turn 18. While this can initially feel disappointing, many students successfully improve their grades during college.

Perhaps the biggest change in recent years has been the growing recognition that success comes in many different forms. University is no longer viewed as the only prestigious route after school. Degree apprenticeships, higher apprenticeships and technical qualifications now offer opportunities to earn a salary while gaining nationally recognised qualifications, often avoiding the student debt associated with traditional university study.

For parents, experts recommend focusing on support rather than pressure. Results day can be emotional regardless of the outcome. Celebrating achievements, discussing options calmly and remembering that there are always alternative pathways can help young people make confident decisions about their future.

Whether a student achieves straight grade 9s or faces unexpected disappointment, GCSE results represent the beginning of the next chapter rather than the end of the story. Across Rochdale borough this summer, thousands of young people will take their next step towards sixth form, college, apprenticeships, employment or technical training—and for many, the opportunities available today are broader than ever before.
